theme: O God, you are my God; earnestly I seek you
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 63. David prays in the wilderness of Judah. Read it as a song of longing and satisfaction. Notice how much it says about desire for God.
settingTheScene: The title reads, “A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah.” This may refer to the days when he fled from Saul, or when he fled from Absalom and crossed the wilderness near the Jordan (2 Samuel 15:23; 16:2, 14). Today it fits well with the last reading. A king in exile, with nothing, finds that he still has what matters most.
observation: “O God, you are my God; earnestly I seek you; my soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you, as in a dry and weary land where there is no water” (v. 1).
“So I have looked upon you in the sanctuary, beholding your power and glory” (v. 2).
“Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you” (v. 3).
“So I will bless you as long as I live; in your name I will lift up my hands” (v. 4).
“My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips” (v. 5).
“When I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night” (v. 6).
“For you have been my help, and in the shadow of your wings I sing for joy” (v. 7).
“My soul clings to you; your right hand upholds me” (v. 8).
interpretation:
The setting is a desert, and the images are thirst and hunger. David has lost his palace, his bed, and his table. Yet in the wilderness he finds that what he truly wants is God himself. “My soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you.” It is the language of deep desire. This is not a lukewarm interest in religion. It is the longing of someone who knows he cannot live without God.

He remembers the sanctuary. He has seen God’s glory there. The memory of worship sustains him in a place where there is no sanctuary. Past experiences of God, stored in the heart, can carry us through dry seasons. This is why corporate worship and memory matter.

The central statement is verse 3: “Your steadfast love is better than life.” This is an extraordinary claim. David loves life. Yet he declares that God’s love is better. It is the confession of a man who has been stripped of everything except God and has found it to be enough. In the Bible, the greatest good is not life, comfort, or safety, but God’s steadfast love.

The satisfaction he describes in verse 5 is the answer to the thirst in verse 1. In the desert he is feasting. The paradox is that those who thirst for God are satisfied by him. He meditates on God in the night, lifting his hands in the darkness. He senses the shelter of God’s wings, a picture of a parent bird.

Verse 8 balances the whole psalm: “My soul clings to you; your right hand upholds me.” There is a double movement. David clings, and God holds. Faith is a grasping, and also a being held. Both are true.
connection: Jesus said, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6), and “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). Philippians 3:8 shows Paul counting everything as loss for the sake of knowing Christ. Jesus also went into the wilderness and drew near to the Father (Luke 5:16). Revelation 7:16-17 promises that the redeemed will no more hunger or thirst.
application:
Ask if your desire for God is a thirst, or only a habit. Ask him to increase it.

In the next dry or lonely time, recall a moment when you knew God’s presence.

Say aloud, “Your steadfast love is better than life.” Where do you struggle to believe it?
prayerPrompts: Tell God what your soul thirsts for.
Tell him that his love is better than life, and why.
Ask him to uphold you as you cling to him.
